Abalone poaching

By: Annalise Lubbe | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Rampant poaching of wild abalone could drive the shellfish to extinction in South Africa within a decade. Carte Blanche investigates.

Unique Selling Point:
A booming illegal trade in abalone is fueling the social and environmental crisis in South Africa. It is estimated that illegal harvesting of abalone from South African shores comprise more than 90% of total abalone production with an estimated value, after processing, of more than R1 billion. Poachers are making 440 million dollars a year by trafficking these giant sea snails into Asia where they are valued as a delicacy. As a result the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries says that “only an appreciable reduction in removals can prevent a complete collapse in the wild within about a decade”.


Summary:
It is Friday midday and yet another news story hit the newsstand: “Law enforcement officials confiscated abalone worth more than R700 000 and arrested 11 suspected poachers in Simon’s Town.” Almost weekly, news flashes appear in the media reporting on illegal poaching on our cape shores: From Pearly Beach to Houtbay, our seas are stripped clean to satisfy an ever growing demand in Asia for the product.

An estimated 4000 tonnes of abalone is caught illegally every year in South Africa. This is 20 times over the limit (98 tonnes per year) set by the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry.

South Africa is one of the largest suppliers to the East where abalone is used as an aphrodisiac, for medicinal purposes and consumed as a delicacy. With their own seas stripped bare seafood suppliers will pay up to R1500 per kilogram of fresh abalone and plated in a Cantonese restaurant, roughly R3 000.

Abalone is run by local and Chinese crime syndicates and gang members like the 26 and 28 gangs. They lure the local fishing community and their families into their network: from divers to spotters, collectors, drivers, sellers and buyers, the industry is highly organised and sophisticated as money is no object. Small communities and towns have been infiltrated and lately even drugs have been used to pay for the abalone which has had a devastating effect on the lives of people.

On the Overberg coast in towns like Pearly Beach, Kleinbaai and Hawston poachers have become so brazen that groups of up to 20 divers will enter the sea during broad daylight and even give you the finger when trying to film them as seen here on a cellphone video clip taken from the deck of a B&B in Hermanus.


Further information:
Nelia Mulder, a local resident from Pearly Beach said Jeanine Taylor said they fear for their safety as poachers have taken the law in their own hands. “Poachers are so arrogant now that they are walking down the street or being dropped off in full diving gear in broad daylight to dive for perlemoen”.

Meet Howard Matinka, a reformed poacher from Hawston near Hernanus who will tell you that he has turned to poaching ‘because our livelihood has been taken away from us. We can’t feed our families, so what is a man to do but poach to stay alive’, he laments. He will introduce us to other locals who are in the same boat.

“Graham’ will tell us more about how the syndicates operate. He worked for Russel Jacobs, a notorious perlemoen syndicate form the Cape underworld. Jacobs faced a string of charges of perlemoen smuggling and organized crime related charges at the of his murder last year. Graham was lured into the world when he was living in a one room garage with wife and child and had to find an income. He was offered a job by Jacobs and soon was top of his game where he organized transport and delivery of abalone, selling to the chines syndicates and a string of other high responsible jobs for which he was paid R20 000 per month, a far cry from the R1000 which he used to earn. He has turned state witness an moved from the Cape to Gautent. He will be talking to us on cellphone and his identity will not be revealed.


More information
Key concerns are:
Small scale fishers are not receiving the same quota as in the past for abalone catch and had to turn to poaching to get by. Secondly, they are intimidated by the onslaught of gangs linked to abalone poaching and feel they don’t have the arm of the law to protect them.

The sale of confiscated illegally obtained abalone by DAFF for far below the market value has resulted in the local market for abalone becoming less competitive for other sellers. There is also no quality standard that the abalone has to meet before it is sold by DAFF which results in a sub standard abalone sold to international markets.

Poaching has reached pitch fever as there are no dedicated operations in place by SAPS, Marine Coastal Management and the SANDF. In the past daily patrols of the western cape coastline by well trained and equipped conservation officers combatted poaching. Today there are no high level collaborative efforts from the various governmental organisations to fight illegal harvesting of abalone. There are also rumours that the police are involved or in some instances turning a blind eye.

Press Release:


Abalone Poaching
Abalone poaching is rampant and it’s driving shellfish to extinction in South Africa. We catch poachers redhanded,
brazenly diving in broad daylight with bags of abalone. Carte Blanche asks: why are authorities
still struggling to get this illegal trade under control?

Script:


Script: Abalone poaching FINAL WITH VIEWING CHANGES
Date: 16 November 2017
Duration: 8 Minutes

Up Music

V/O It is Saturday morning in Pearly Beach, 23 km from Gangsbaai in the Western Cape. Stretched out for miles are unspoilt coastline and a rich marine life. Paradise it seems, or not?

V/O We zoom in with our drone. In the shallow water amongst the kelp we spot a pair of blue flippers, then the bag, and then the tool. An abalone poacher it seems. Where there is one there must be more. Yes. 8 more on the rocks shucking their abalone, removing the shells and filling their bags.

Up music.

V/O Then they spot the drone and head out of the water and into the bushes. We hover above. They ditch the bags with their loot and start running to get away from the drone. But we are hot on their heals. We track them to the other side of the beach where they pile into a waiting taxi. In response from an anonymous call a vehicle from the Department of Fisheries arrive. One of the team jumps on board to film the chase.

Audio up: Why can’t SAPS get here?

V/O This is where Fisheries turn around. They would not dare going into the township without backup it seems. In the meantime our drone stayed peeled on the bushes where the abalone was stashed. Five guys appear out of nowhere. They start looking for the abalone but make a run when they realised they have been spotted.

Up music

V/O We return to the spot where the bags were stashed. Within minutes 8 bags of abalone are retrieved.



Up audio: I can’t believe the size.

V/O It is with a shock that we found that most of the abalone in the bag was between 1 and 3 years old. Small babies that have not even reached maturity.

Up music

V/O The scene that you just witness is a daily occurrence here in Pearly Beach. The local community speaks strongly against the criminal element that has taken over but they feel helpless and vulnerable. A local resident who fears for her safety has asked that we hide her identity.

Local resident; We sit on our verandah at the ocean and we watch all this happen and we have nobody that you can report it to. 50, 60 at a time, 20, 30 boats going out. You do feel unsafe and intimidated.

John: You have to ask where are the police . Why are they not doing their job?

Local resident: The police claim it is not their job to catch the poachers. DAFF who is suppose to be the main people doing the policing they are outnumbered and outpowered.

V/O It is estimated that 4000 tonnes of abalone is caught illegally every year in South Africa. This is 20 times the legal limit set by the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries. At this rate we will deplete our natural resource within the next 10 years.

V/O Deputy Minister, Bheki Cele claims they are under-staffed and do not have the capacity to control the coastline with their limited resources.

Bheki Cele: Deputy Minister Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries: We have little bit more than 200 people that take care of our coast of 3200 km. we have only 4 vessels to look after that; we are trying to increase our own capacity.

Up audio: What happens to the abalone now?

Daff officer: it goes to the police station into storage

V/O Abalone once confiscated eventually makes its way back to DAFF who sell it back into the market and the profits they gain, they say is pumped back into their budget to fight crime.

John: DAFF sells confiscated abalone. Isn’t that like selling a stolen motorcar and then operate on that level?

General Bheki Cele: I believe that everything sold comes back. I do have that that syndicates buy the stuff and then legalise it but the principal of the system for me is right that get the money to fight crime but the actual practice I could not guarantee.

V/O We head for Hawston north of Pearly Beach where we meet Howard Matinka, a reformed poacher who came from generations of fishers.

Howard Matinka: Reformed poacher. That time fish was so plentiful, even here Hawston, we call it the boesman skuitjies and we just catch and catch and catch. But we are suffering now.

V/O Matinka, like so many other small scale fishers has had a raw deal from the Department of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries who grant the permits. He has simply been ignored. Of the 277 abalone catch permits issued for 2017 small scale fishers received none. Poverty has driven many individuals to illegal poaching as a means to put food on the table. And this in turned created a network of gang-related activities and organised crime.

John: so what impact has that had on Hawston, how has it changed this town?

Howard Matinka: it has changed this town, the big bosses that is behind it, the big criminals like smuggling drugs. The whole system, maybe the cops is involved.

John: Give us an idea how bad the situation is at the moment with poaching

Howard Matinka: In my time the poachers wasn’t so in the gangsters hands. But then the gangsters came on board. They are controlling it with an iron fist.

V/O The abalone trade is booming and at the head of the business are Chinese and local syndicates and organised gangs competing in the illegal trade of wild abalone.

Up audio:

V/O Charles, not his real name, worked for one of the most notorious abalone syndicate bosses from the Cape underworld who has since been gunned down. Charles was put in charge of smuggling, transporting and selling the white gold. He has gone into hiding.

John Webb: Who was buying this abalone, do you have any idea of who the end customers were or was it purely middlemen that you dealt with.

Charles: Ex-syndicate member: Dit was meeste die chinese wat die perlemoen koop. (It was mainly the Chinese that bought the abalone) Ons middelmanne het gedeel met mekaar en die base het gedeel met mekaar. (We middlemen dealt with one another and the bosses dealt with each other)

V/O Charles explained in detail the typical workings of an operation.

Charles: Op n werksaand daar is 3 organisasies wat werk daai aand (On a week night there is three teams that work that night), elke organisasie het about 25 duikers so dink by jouself (Each team comprises of 25 divers so think for yourself), nou praat ek nie eers van die transporters en die lookouts so dis n helse operasie. (Now that is not to mention the transporters and the spotters…so it is a big operation)

V/O Charles handles roughly 75 divers per shift. Each diver takes out roughly 12 kilos. Abalone is sold at about R450 per kilo. This equals R405 000 for one shift’s work at a typical fishing community on a coastline that stretches for 320km from Pearly Beach to Houtbay.

V/O It is clear that there is little or no effective enforcement and policing of abalone poaching. and there seems to be no end to the destruction on an industrial scale that will eventually lead to the extinction of the wild abalone in this pristine coastal region.

Up song

V/O Whole communities have been under siege by syndicates and gangsters who have enriched themselves and marginalised the local population with their illegal abalone poaching.

Matinka: Hawston is angry, they are angry. Hawston is like a time bomb it is just a matter of time when the people is going to stamp their foot down and say enough is now enough.

(It was mainly the Chinese that bought the abalone) Ons middelmanne het gedeel met mekaar en die base het gedeel met mekaar. (We middlemen dealt with one another and the bosses dealt with each other) V/O Charles explained in detail the typical workings of an operation. Charles: Op n werksaand daar is 3 organisasies wat werk daai aand (On a week night there is three teams that work that night), elke organisasie het about 25 duikers so dink by jouself (Each team comprises of 25 divers so think for yourself), nou praat ek nie eers van die transporters en die lookouts so dis n helse operasie. (Now that is not to mention the transporters and the spotters…so it is a big operation) V/O Charles handles roughly 75 divers per shift. Each diver takes out roughly 12 kilos. Abalone is sold at about R450 per kilo. This equals R405 000 for one shift’s work at a typical fishing community on a coastline that stretches for 320km from Pearly Beach to Houtbay. V/O It is clear that there is little or no effective enforcement and policing of abalone poaching. and there seems to be no end to the destruction on an industrial scale that will eventually lead to the extinction of the wild abalone in this pristine coastal region. Up song V/O Whole communities have been under siege by syndicates and gangsters who have enriched themselves and marginalised the local population with their illegal abalone poaching. Matinka: Hawston is angry, they are angry. Hawston is like a time bomb it is just a matter of time when the people is going to stamp their foot down and say enough is now enough. _______________________________________________________________________ Promos: 10 second: V/O It is estimated that 4000 tonnes of abalone is caught illegally every year. HThat is 20 times the legal limit. At this rate we will deplete our natural resource within the next 10 years. 15 second: V/O Poverty has driven many fishers to abalone poaching. And this in turn created a network of gang-related activities and organised crime. Howard Matinka: in my time the poachers wasn’t so in the gangsters hands it was ordinary people. But then the gangsters came on board and now it is in their hands. They are controlling it with an iron fist. 15 second V/O From Houtbay to Pearly Beach very town is under siege with the onslaught of poachers Local resident: We sit on our verandah at the ocean and we watch all this happen and we have nobody that you can report it to. 50, 60 at a time.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Rampant poaching of wild abalone could drive the shellfish to extinction in South Africa within a decade. Carte Blanche investigates.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A booming illegal trade in abalone is fueling the social and environmental crisis in South Africa. It is estimated that illegal harvesting of abalone from South African shores comprise more than 90% of total abalone production with an estimated value, after processing, of more than R1 billion. Poachers are making 440 million dollars a year by trafficking these giant sea snails into Asia where they are valued as a delicacy. As a result the Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries says that “only an appreciable reduction in removals can prevent a complete collapse in the wild within about a decade”.
metadata.Summary: It is Friday midday and yet another news story hit the newsstand: “Law enforcement officials confiscated abalone worth more than R700 000 and arrested 11 suspected poachers in Simon’s Town.” Almost weekly, news flashes appear in the media reporting on illegal poaching on our cape shores: From Pearly Beach to Houtbay, our seas are stripped clean to satisfy an ever growing demand in Asia for the product. An estimated 4000 tonnes of abalone is caught illegally every year in South Africa. This is 20 times over the limit (98 tonnes per year) set by the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. South Africa is one of the largest suppliers to the East where abalone is used as an aphrodisiac, for medicinal purposes and consumed as a delicacy. With their own seas stripped bare seafood suppliers will pay up to R1500 per kilogram of fresh abalone and plated in a Cantonese restaurant, roughly R3 000. Abalone is run by local and Chinese crime syndicates and gang members like the 26 and 28 gangs. They lure the local fishing community and their families into their network: from divers to spotters, collectors, drivers, sellers and buyers, the industry is highly organised and sophisticated as money is no object. Small communities and towns have been infiltrated and lately even drugs have been used to pay for the abalone which has had a devastating effect on the lives of people. On the Overberg coast in towns like Pearly Beach, Kleinbaai and Hawston poachers have become so brazen that groups of up to 20 divers will enter the sea during broad daylight and even give you the finger when trying to film them as seen here on a cellphone video clip taken from the deck of a B&B in Hermanus.
metadata.Further information: Nelia Mulder, a local resident from Pearly Beach said Jeanine Taylor said they fear for their safety as poachers have taken the law in their own hands. “Poachers are so arrogant now that they are walking down the street or being dropped off in full diving gear in broad daylight to dive for perlemoen”. Meet Howard Matinka, a reformed poacher from Hawston near Hernanus who will tell you that he has turned to poaching ‘because our livelihood has been taken away from us. We can’t feed our families, so what is a man to do but poach to stay alive’, he laments. He will introduce us to other locals who are in the same boat. “Graham’ will tell us more about how the syndicates operate. He worked for Russel Jacobs, a notorious perlemoen syndicate form the Cape underworld. Jacobs faced a string of charges of perlemoen smuggling and organized crime related charges at the of his murder last year. Graham was lured into the world when he was living in a one room garage with wife and child and had to find an income. He was offered a job by Jacobs and soon was top of his game where he organized transport and delivery of abalone, selling to the chines syndicates and a string of other high responsible jobs for which he was paid R20 000 per month, a far cry from the R1000 which he used to earn. He has turned state witness an moved from the Cape to Gautent. He will be talking to us on cellphone and his identity will not be revealed. More information Key concerns are: Small scale fishers are not receiving the same quota as in the past for abalone catch and had to turn to poaching to get by. Secondly, they are intimidated by the onslaught of gangs linked to abalone poaching and feel they don’t have the arm of the law to protect them. The sale of confiscated illegally obtained abalone by DAFF for far below the market value has resulted in the local market for abalone becoming less competitive for other sellers. There is also no quality standard that the abalone has to meet before it is sold by DAFF which results in a sub standard abalone sold to international markets. Poaching has reached pitch fever as there are no dedicated operations in place by SAPS, Marine Coastal Management and the SANDF. In the past daily patrols of the western cape coastline by well trained and equipped conservation officers combatted poaching. Today there are no high level collaborative efforts from the various governmental organisations to fight illegal harvesting of abalone. There are also rumours that the police are involved or in some instances turning a blind eye.
